newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Exporters must wait for gains from low NZD-experts.
newsitem.headline: Exporters must wait for gains from low NZD-experts.

text.p: New Zealand exporters may have to wait a while before they see the benefits of the currency's recent slide, analysts said on Monday.

Treasurer Winston Peters said on Friday the kiwi dollar was likely to stay down for some months and exporters, who had battled with a high currency for the past two years, were well placed to take advantage of the competitive edge that offered.

"The government believes exporters are in a strong position to bounce back after the recent fall in the value of the currency, because you've toughened yourselves up while the dollar was high," Peters said in speech notes for an address to the Export Institute of New Zealand.
The kiwi has slid to 64.3 U.S. cents from a year high of 71.1 cents in January. However, exporters are not yet popping the champagne corks.
"Farmers are waiting for prices to improve," Federated Farmers president Malcolm Bailey told Reuters.

"Some are asking as recently as today why the meat schedules (prices) haven't risen a bit as the dollar has come down. It was a little bit disappointing too that the season's first wool sale didn't seem to reflect the new level of the dollar," he said.
Andrew Powers, spokesman for meat processing company Affco Holdings Ltd, said the sustainability of the kiwi's weakness was the key to benefits feeding through the economy.
The meat industry would not experience a large impact unless the currency managed to remain at low levels until October, when there is a seasonal pick-up in the meat business, he said.
Bancorp Treasury Services, which has many exporter clients, doubted the kiwi's fall was sustainable.
"This is only a correction to an otherwise long term up-trend," economist Stuart Marshall said. "I don't think it's a change of direction...we're still a very strong economy."
Marshall said Bancorp was advising its clients to increase forward cover in order to protect themselves against the type of rapid currency appreciation that hurt so many exporters in 1996.
However, ANZ Investment Bank chief economist Paul Stewart told Reuters Financial Television sentiment for the kiwi remained clearly on the downside.

"We'd be looking for it to ease further -- the TWI (Trade-Weighted Index) I think will come down by another index point or so at least, and that would provide scope for the kiwi to fall to under 64 (U.S.) cents in due course," he said.
Stewart said the export sector's relief would in time flow through to the rest of the economy, creating more sustainable growth heading into 1998.
National Bank of New Zealand chief economist Brendan O'Donovan agreed.

He said that at present, much of the impetus for growth in 1998 was coming from tax cuts and higher government spending. That could prompt a consumption-based economic recovery, which tended to be less sustainable.

"So the decline in the kiwi dollar is very good news, because it will make the growth profile going forward a lot more balanced than it otherwise would have been, and by implication longer-lasting," O'Donovan said.
He said exporters should start to see the weaker currency help boost incomes in three to six months.
